title: Visualization of Cortex Organization and Dynamics in Microorganisms, using Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence Microscopy
protocol: Clean coverslips from dust particles using forceps.
Place coverslips in a ceramic holder with lid.
Fill glass container with 1 M NaOH.
Incubate coverslips under slow continuous rotation for 2 hours.
Wash coverslips twice with distilled water for 5 minutes each under slow continuous rotation.
Store washed coverslips in a ceramic holder covered in 100% ethanol.
Dilute Bacillus subtilis cells to an OD600 of 0.01 - 0.05 in 5 ml of appropriate growth media.
Grow diluted cells to exponential phase (OD600 of 0.3-0.7).
Prepare 1.25% agarose in water or medium using synthetic media for reduced background fluorescence.
Dissolve agarose powder in a 1.5 ml plastic tube at 95°C and store in heating block at 72°C.
Add a small drop of agarose to the middle of a slide and press into a flat pad with a second slide.
Carefully separate slides after at least 2 minutes or before use.
Spin down 500 μl cells in micro centrifuge at 12.000 rpm for 1 minute.
Discard supernatant, resuspend pellet in 50 μl medium.
Add 2-4 μl cells to the center of the agarose pad.
Take a cleaned coverslip from the ethanol filled container with forceps and dry it with pressurized air.
Carefully place the dried coverslip on the sample.
Let cells settle for at least 2 minutes prior to microscopy.
Take a coverslip from the container with forceps and dry with pressurized air.
Spread 5 μl Concanavalin A solution (ConA, 2 μg/ml in distilled water) on cover slip with a pipette and dry with pressurized air.
Transfer 4.5 μl yeast cell suspension to one side of the ConA-coated coverslip.
Carefully place cover slip on microscope slide starting with one edge and let drop slowly to avoid formation of air bubbles.
Let cells settle for at least 2 min prior to microscopy.
Seal edges of coverslip with VALAP (Vaseline, Lanolin and Parafin, mixed at equal weight under heat, apply with small brush or spatula) for long term imaging.
Set up a customized Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence (TIRF) microscope on an automated iMIC stand.
Use 75 mW DPSS lasers at 488 nm and 561 nm as light sources.
Select lasers through an AOTF and direct them to the iMIC via a broadband fiber.
Adjust incidence angles or FRAP position using a galvanometer-driven two-axis scanner head.
Switch between epifluorescence, TIRF, and FRAP modes with an additional galvanometer.
Capture images with an Andor iXON DU-897 EMCCD camera equipped with a 2x magnification lens.
Control acquisition through the Live Acquisition software package by Till Photonics.
Use an Olympus 100x NA 1.45 objective for Objective-type TIRF imaging.
Place a 2x magnification lens in front of the EMCCD camera to maintain maximum resolution.
Adjust environmental controls to keep cells under optimal growth conditions during imaging.
Utilize a custom-made heating chamber to study yeast temperature-sensitive mutants.
Employ simple flow chambers or glass-bottom culture dishes for medium exchange during acquisition.
Identify position of cells using bright field illumination.
Switch to laser illumination and select appropriate lasers and filter combinations to excite the fluorophores of choice.
Set TIRF angle to 0° to obtain a perpendicular laser beam if unsure.
Find the top section of the cell (side facing the coverslip).
Alter the incident angle of the laser beam until signals disappear, then slowly increase the angle until fluorescence at the cell surface reappears.
Adjust z-focus for optimal position at the cell surface.
Save the TIRF angle and move to an unbleached stage position if significant photo bleaching occurs during setup.
Adjust laser intensities and camera gain to maximize dynamic range without saturating pixels.
Focus on the z-position used for TIRF imaging.
Remove the sample from the objective.
Clean the objective of all oil.
Project the laser on the ceiling in TIRF mode.
Calibrate the 0° position such that the laser is in a straight line with the objective.
Wear laser safety goggles and avoid all reflections in the beam path.
Focus the laser spot to a minimal size.
Use a moveable lens positioned between galvos and microscope for calibration.
Perform calibration before every session.
